Field feedback / annotated walkthrough

What sales teams say they don't need in MERIT

Marked up against the screens as they stand today, based on structured walkthroughs with hotel sales and revenue-management contacts — consistent with a pattern across roughly a dozen conversations to date. Red marks what these conversations say should come out or shrink drastically; amber marks an area that needs reshaping or filling in, rather than removal.

SourcesField walkthroughs with hotel sales & revenue-management contacts · ~12 conversations to date
PatternNot one or two data points — feedback below repeats across the broader conversation set
Cut / simplify heavily — not trusted or not used as designed
Keep, but rework — valued, needs to be reshaped

01 — Dashboard

Dashboard & scoring rail

The default landing screen, and the one carrying the most criticized surface area: a ranking model, a six-way score panel, and win/pickup percentages down every row.

1
2
3
4
5
6

The Score and Win/Pickup columns repeat this way for all 35 queued RFPs below the fold.

  1. 1

    New RFP Cut

    Manual entry is a nonstarter — the sales system has to stay the system of record and feed MERIT automatically. This button sits on every screen.

  2. 2

    Ranking control Cut

    With ~48-hour SLAs, reps are accountable for the whole queue and mostly work it by date received — ranking by score isn't a real workflow. Re-ranking also didn't reliably move opportunities when we changed parameters in testing.

  3. 3

    Score column Cut

    The number doesn't mean anything to reps — the most consistent piece of feedback so far. They want a simple good / neutral / bad read, with the reasoning available on click or hover.

  4. 4

    Win % / Pickup % Cut

    Not trusted, not useful. Experienced sellers feel they already know which leads are serious — another percentage doesn't change their read.

  5. 5

    All Method Scores Cut

    Six overlapping scoring methods on one opportunity is more than anyone will use. This is the density problem in miniature.

  6. 6

    Displacement Cut

    Displacement matters, but reps already trust their RMS's number for it. Surface that instead of running a parallel MERIT calculation.

05 — Trends

Trends & historical reporting

Property-wide revenue, segment and pacing charts across 2023–2025.

1
  1. 1

    Trends Rework

    The one screen people got genuinely interested in — but as a standalone report, not tied to any specific deal. They want this simplified and reoriented around the opportunity they're actually evaluating: prior-year ADR and room nights for those dates, current group OTB, transient forecast, room vs. F&B/meeting revenue, win/loss history. Worth noting: a lot of this base reporting already exists in their other systems, so the value is in assembling it around the deal, not re-reporting it.

06 — Edit RFP

Pricing strategy panel

The per-opportunity view: RFP details on the left, three generated pricing strategies on the right.

1
2
  1. 1

    Three pricing strategies Cut

    Three full options is more than reps want to weigh under time pressure. The ask is one recommendation — a rate and F&B minimum — with the reference points behind it, and room to flex the inputs themselves and see what happens to the deal.

  2. 2

    Win Prob. / Deal Score Cut

    Same untrusted win-probability and unexplained score baked into every option. Recommended concessions land the same way — reps already know what they're authorized to offer and what the client asked for.

07 — APIT / Nexus data-source spec

What the parameter plan still needs to resolve

The same field conversations, checked against the parameter-by-data-source plan for the next build. No screen to mark up here — these are gaps in the plan itself, plus one place it quietly brings back something reps already rejected.

  1. 1

    “Win probability indicators” as an output Cut

    Still listed as something the engine produces — the same untrusted metric flagged on the dashboard above. If it stays backend-only, feeding the recommendation without being shown, that's fine; as written it reads like it's meant to be surfaced to the rep again.

  2. 2

    Meeting space & catering inventory Add

    Nothing in the plan supplies function-space holds or banquet/catering pricing, yet "available meeting space" and a rate + F&B-minimum recommendation both depend on it. Needs its own source — a catering/event module or space-management tool.

  3. 3

    Concession & rate authorization limits Add

    The ask was to let reps plug in what they're authorized to offer and see what happens to the deal, not receive a recommended concession. That needs a source for negotiating boundaries — rate floor, comp-room limit, F&B discount ceiling — currently absent from the plan.

  4. 4

    Win/loss history above the account level Add

    The CRM source only gives win/loss for this specific account. The field asked for how deals like this one — same segment, similar lead time — usually go. That's a derived aggregate across CRM and RFP history, not currently modeled anywhere.

  5. 5

    Two more flags worth adding Add

    A decision-deadline-approaching flag, distinct from a slow start at intake, and an F&B minimum well below typical for the group's size and type — the natural counterpart to the low-ADR flag already planned.

  6. 6

    Sync cadence per source Add

    APIT still ingests PMS on-books data to compute availability-adjacent fields. Given how emphatic the field was that availability can't drift even slightly, freshness per source deserves a stated SLA rather than an assumed live feed.

  7. 7

    Group-type taxonomy alignment Add

    RFP intake, Knowland benchmarks, and PMS historicals need to use the same segment categories, or the "comparable deals" comps this plan depends on won't actually line up.

The open question

Decision support, not a decision-maker

"How does this opportunity fit into our overall revenue strategy for these dates, why does it fit, and if it doesn't, what would need to change to make it work?"

That's the question people keep circling back to — and it's a different product than a tool that ranks, scores and recommends a rate on a rep's behalf. It's also raised a second, bigger question worth sitting with before we keep building: whether the salesperson is even the right primary user, or whether MERIT's analysis is worth more at the DOS/RM/GM or corporate level, with a much simpler view for the person actually answering the RFP.

— paraphrased from the team call, Aug 27 2026
